`Inference:` If “most consequential” means “most emphasized by Bun’s own official release materials,” the top changes are probably: **the Rust rewrite**, **the large Node.js compatibility jump**, **the runtime/performance improvements**, and **the new built-in standard-library features/tools**. # Bun 1.4: Major Release Summary

**Publication Date:** August 20, 2026

## Most Consequential Changes

### Complete Rust Rewrite
The biggest structural change is that Bun has been entirely rewritten from Zig to Rust. This is the first production release, though internal tools like Claude Code have been using the Rust version for months.

### Performance Improvements
The release delivers dramatic efficiency gains:
- **CPU usage:** Production CPU dropped by 2× for large applications; idle CPU usage decreased by 5×
- **Memory:** HTTP server applications see 13–48% memory reductions (Fastify down 48%, Express down 46%)
- **Startup:** Windows startup is 2.5× faster; Linux startup is 2× faster with less than half the memory
- **Binary size:** Reductions up to 17% on Linux and Windows

### Node.js Compatibility Surge
Bun added 1,517 newly passing tests from the Node.js test suite—its biggest compatibility jump since version 1.0. Critical modules like `node:http`, `node:fs`, and `node:stream` now pass approximately 97% of Node's tests.

### Built-in Standard Library
Fifteen previously external dependencies are now integrated:

> "Every one of these ships in the Bun binary — no install step, no native build, no lockfile entry"

New APIs include `Bun.Image`, `Bun.WebView`, `Bun.markdown`, `Bun.cron()`, `Bun.Terminal`, and `Bun.Archive`, alongside expanded utilities for JSON/XML parsing and terminal operations.

### Testing & Building Enhancements
- `bun test --parallel` distributes test files across worker processes
- `bun test --shard` enables distributed CI testing
- Built-in React Compiler runs 19× faster than Babel plugin equivalents
- `bun run --parallel` executes scripts concurrently with output prefixing

### Developer Tooling
New observability features include `--cpu-prof-md` and `--heap-prof-md` for Markdown-formatted profiling reports readable over SSH or in terminals, plus `process.on("memoryPressure")` for OS-level memory notifications.

## Breaking Changes/Migration Notes

The post does not explicitly mention breaking changes or migration notes. It focuses on new features rather than compatibility issues.

## Global Virtual Store & Install Speed

The post states: **"On a warm isolated install, copying packages into `node_modules` (`clonefileat()` on macOS) was 95% of main-thread time"** and reports that **"on the common CI path (lockfile present, cache warm, `node_modules` wiped), a 1,400-package install is 7x faster."**

The feature uses symlinks instead of copies, but it's opt-in: **"The global store is opt-in: it applies when you select the isolated linker, which is not the default for existing projects."**

## Windows ARM64 Support

The post includes binary size comparisons showing Windows ARM64: **"75.1 MB"** for Bun 1.4, down from **"90.2 MB"** in 1.3.14. It's listed among supported platforms but receives no special discussion of new support.

## Built-in APIs Replacing npm Packages

The post lists 15 dependencies now built-in:

- **`Bun.Image`** replaces **sharp**
- **`Bun.WebView`** replaces **puppeteer**
- **`Bun.markdown`** replaces **marked**
- **`Bun.cron()`** replaces **node-cron**
- **`Bun.Terminal`** replaces **node-pty**
- **`bun run --parallel`** replaces **concurrently** and **npm-run-all**

Plus replacements for json5, fast-xml-parser, tar, string-width, slice-ansi, cli-truncate, and wrap-ansi.

## Latest stable Bun release: **v1.4.0**

**Version and date (supported fact).** Bun v1.4.0 is the current latest stable release. It is marked "Latest" on GitHub's releases page with a publication date of August 20, 2026 ([github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/latest](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/latest), [releases list](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases)), and the official announcement post on the Bun blog is dated August 20, 2026 ([bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4), [bun.com/blog](https://bun.com/blog)). Independently, the npm registry's `latest` dist-tag for the `bun` package resolves to `1.4.0` ([registry.npmjs.org/bun/latest](https://registry.npmjs.org/bun/latest)).

**No patch release yet (supported, with a caveat).** As of today (2026-08-27), no 1.4.x patch has shipped: GitHub lists v1.4.0 as the newest release, with v1.3.14 (May 13, 2026) before it, and npm still points `latest` at 1.4.0 ([GitHub releases](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases), [bun.com/blog](https://bun.com/blog), [npm](https://registry.npmjs.org/bun/latest)). Caveat: fetched pages may be cached, so a very recent patch could be missed.

**Minor date disagreement.** endoflife.date lists the 1.4.0 release date as August 19, 2026 ([endoflife.date/bun](https://endoflife.date/bun)), one day earlier than GitHub and the official blog. I trust the official sources; the discrepancy is most plausibly a timezone artifact — that last part is my inference, not something any source states.

### Most consequential changes, per the official announcement

All of the following come from the official release post at [bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4):

- **Bun is rewritten from Zig to Rust.** 1.4.0 is the first production release of the Rust implementation; the post says internal tools including Claude Code had been running it for months. This is the headline structural change.
- **Large runtime efficiency gains.** Production CPU usage dropped ~2× for large applications and idle CPU ~5×; HTTP server memory fell 13–48% (Fastify −48%, Express −46%); startup is 2.5× faster on Windows and 2× faster on Linux; binary size shrank up to 17% (e.g. Windows ARM64 from 90.2 MB to 75.1 MB).
- **Biggest Node.js compatibility jump since 1.0:** 1,517 newly passing Node.js test-suite tests, with `node:http`, `node:fs`, and `node:stream` at roughly 97% pass rates.
- **Fifteen common npm dependencies absorbed into the binary**, including `Bun.Image` (replacing sharp), `Bun.WebView` (puppeteer), `Bun.markdown` (marked), `Bun.cron()` (node-cron), `Bun.Terminal` (node-pty), `bun run --parallel` (concurrently / npm-run-all), plus `Bun.Archive` and replacements for json5, fast-xml-parser, tar, string-width, slice-ansi, cli-truncate, and wrap-ansi. The post's framing: "Every one of these ships in the Bun binary — no install step, no native build, no lockfile entry."
- **Faster installs via a global virtual store**, using symlinks instead of copies. On the common CI path (lockfile present, cache warm, `node_modules` wiped), a 1,400-package install is **7× faster**. Important qualifier stated in the post: this is **opt-in** — it applies only when you select the isolated linker, "which is not the default for existing projects."
- **Testing and tooling:** `bun test --parallel` (worker processes) and `--shard` for distributed CI, a built-in React Compiler said to be 19× faster than the Babel plugin, Markdown-format profiling output (`--cpu-prof-md`, `--heap-prof-md`), and `process.on("memoryPressure")`.

### Where evidence is thin

- **Breaking changes / migration.** The announcement post does not enumerate breaking changes or migration notes — it is framed around new features. Given a full language rewrite, I would *expect* behavioral edge-case differences, but that is inference; I found no official statement either confirming or denying breaking changes, so treat "drop-in upgrade" as unverified.
- **Windows ARM64.** A search result summary described Windows ARM64 as a new capability in 1.4, but the official post only shows it in a binary-size table without announcing it as new. I can't confirm the "new platform support" claim from official sources.
- **Context.** The Bun blog lists a December 2, 2025 post announcing that Bun is joining Anthropic ([bun.com/blog](https://bun.com/blog)), and a July 8, 2026 post explaining the Rust rewrite rationale. I did not open either, so I'm reporting only their existence and titles, not their contents.
- One search result (an InfoQ item referencing a "Bun v3.1" release) appears inconsistent with every official source, which show a 1.x line. I did not open it and place no weight on it.
